Troy enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 22-11 overall after finishing 20-11 in the regular season and 12-6 in Sun Belt play, then winning the Sun Belt Tournament with a 78-70 semifinal win over Southern Miss on March 8, 2026 and a 77-61 title-game win over Georgia Southern on March 9, 2026. The regular-season title was outright, secured by an 80-65 home win over ULM on February 27, 2026. Scott Cross was named Sun Belt Coach of the Year after guiding Troy to that 20-11, 12-6 regular-season mark. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/news/2026/2/27/basketball-m-troy-wins-outright-sun-belt-regular-season-title))

From a traditional scouting standpoint, Troy’s offense is built around pressure on the rim, second shots, and multiple ballhandlers rather than one pure table-setter. The numbers show the shape of it: 82.6 points per game in league notes before the conference tournament, 16.0 assists per game for the full season, and a constant rebounding emphasis. Thomas Dowd leads the club in both shot volume at 11.2 field-goal attempts per game and offensive rebounding at 3.1 per game, while Victor Valdes leads in assists at 4.6 per game and free throws made at 5.2 per game. Cooper Campbell adds 4.2 assists per game and is one of three perimeter volume shooters over 5.0 three-point attempts per game, alongside Dowd and Cobi Campbell. That tells you Troy is not a static half-court team; they play through drive-and-kick, hit-ahead pressure, and inside-out work off Dowd’s activity. The clearest game example was the 99-74 home win over Arkansas State on January 17, when Troy piled up 25 assists and Valdes had 17 points with 14 assists. Another was the 90-70 road win at Louisiana on January 10, when six Trojans scored in double figures and Troy demolished Louisiana 42-19 on the glass, including a 24-13 edge in offensive rebounds. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Specific offensive tendencies stand out in game evidence. First, Troy will use Dowd as a trail big and pick-and-pop/pick-and-roll hybrid; he averages 14.8 points, shoots 34.4 percent from three on 189 attempts, and is also the team’s best rebounder. That combination is unusual and forces opposing fives to defend space. Second, Valdes is their downhill foul-drawer; his 220 free-throw attempts in 32 games are by far the team high, and he reached the line 10 times made in the Sun Belt semifinal against Southern Miss, a career high. Third, Troy can flip into a perimeter-heavy game when needed: in the December 14 win at UAB, Cobi Campbell hit his fourth three of the day late, and Troy won 86-85 on Dowd’s buzzer putback after a missed three. Those examples show a team comfortable winning through half-court creation, offensive rebounding, or spread-floor late-clock play. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Defensively, Cross’s teams still look like Cross’s teams: physical man-to-man principles, aggressive work on the glass, and disruption without reckless giveaway fouling. Troy’s season averages show 8.0 steals per game, 3.4 blocks per game, a +3.5 rebounding margin, and opponents at just 34.8 rebounds per game. In the 59-49 win over South Alabama on January 3, Troy survived its own offensive droughts because the defense held the Jaguars to 49 points. In the 61-point title-game defensive effort against Georgia Southern on March 9, Troy limited the opponent to one of its season lows. Jerrell Bellamy’s role is central here as the mobile interior enforcer; he averaged 1.0 block per game for the year and posted 6 blocks against Southern Miss in the Sun Belt semifinal. Dowd adds 1.3 blocks and 1.2 steals per game, giving Troy a front line that can contest at the rim and still clean the possession with a rebound. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Cross’s coaching philosophy is visible in how often Troy changes the winning formula game to game. When the game is fast and chaotic, he leans into depth and toughness. In the November 18 road win at San Diego State, Troy won 108-107 in double overtime despite multiple foul-outs; Cross had to extend Austin Cross and freshman Javen Colbert in overtime, and both delivered, with Austin Cross hitting a clutch overtime three and Colbert making two enormous free throws after his own steal with 23 seconds left. When the game requires a tactical offensive response, Troy can re-balance. After losing 86-74 at Arkansas State on January 7, Cross adjusted in the rematch on January 17: Troy cut its turnovers to seven, assisted on 25 baskets, and won by 25. After a 44-66 home loss to App State on January 31 and a 62-74 loss at Texas State on February 11, Troy closed the regular season 4-1, including a 78-59 win over Louisiana and the title-clinching 80-65 win over ULM. That is documented adjustment history, not theory. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/news/2025/11/19/basketball-m-troy-stuns-san-diego-state-in-double-overtime-thriller-108-107?utm_source=openai))

Late-game execution is a genuine strength. Troy opened the year with a 103-97 overtime road win at Kent State on November 3. On November 18, it beat San Diego State 108-107 in double overtime on the road, with Dowd posting 25 points and 19 rebounds. On December 14, it won at UAB 86-85 when Dowd banked in the winner at the buzzer. On January 21, it won 83-77 in double overtime at Old Dominion. Most revealing for tournament projection was February 18: Troy escaped ULM 77-76 on the road in a one-possession game during a title race. This is not a team shocked by chaos; it has lived in overtime and one-possession finishes all season. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

The key players are defined and productive. Dowd is the centerpiece: 14.8 points, 10.1 rebounds, 2.2 assists, 1.3 blocks, 34.4 percent from three, 79.6 percent at the line, and 16 double-doubles entering postseason awards. His standout games include 25 points and 19 rebounds at San Diego State, plus 23 points and 13 rebounds in the Sun Belt title game against Georgia Southern, which earned tournament MOP honors. Valdes is the slasher-creator: 14.8 points, 4.6 assists, 4.0 rebounds, 167 made free throws, and a signature 17-point, 14-assist double-double against Arkansas State. Theo Seng is the efficient interior scorer at 12.9 points on 51.7 percent shooting. Cooper Campbell is the secondary organizer and spacing guard: 12.7 points, 4.2 assists, 38.6 percent from three, and team-best 1.6 steals per game. Bellamy is the finisher/rim protector, shooting 65.1 percent from the field and exploding for a career-high 25 points against Louisiana on February 24. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

The notable wins tell you Troy’s ceiling. Beating San Diego State 108-107 on November 18 showed the Trojans can survive a rock fight against a physical, high-major-caliber defense. Winning at UAB 86-85 on December 14 showed poise and second-shot toughness. The 90-70 win at Louisiana on January 10 showed their rebounding can flatten a quality league team on the road. The 99-74 blowout of Arkansas State on January 17 showed their best offensive version: 25 assists, low turnovers, and balance. The worst losses reveal the pressure points. The 44-66 home loss to App State on January 31 exposed what happens when Troy’s offense bogs down and the jump shooting dries up. The 65-69 loss at Southern Miss on February 14 and 54-65 loss at South Alabama on February 21 showed that disciplined half-court opponents can drag Troy into lower-possession games. The 63-74 loss at LMU and 85-94 loss at CSUN in November showed that if Troy fails to control tempo and the defensive glass, it can be stretched laterally. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/12/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

As for NCAA Tournament history under Scott Cross, this is his third NCAA Tournament appearance as a head coach. He previously took UT Arlington to the 2008 NCAA Tournament, where the Mavericks lost in the first round, and he led Troy to the 2025 NCAA Tournament, where the Trojans lost to Kentucky in the first round. Troy’s 2026 bid therefore gives Cross another first-round opportunity, and as of the 2025 tournament recap he was 0-2 as a head coach in NCAA Tournament games. Troy the team is making its fourth NCAA Tournament appearance overall, but under Cross specifically, the documented tournament years are 2025 and 2026 at Troy plus 2008 at UT Arlington, with both completed runs ending in the first round. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/news/2025/3/11/basketball-m-troy-earns-berth-in-ncaa-tournament?utm_source=openai))

matchup-analyst:
Troy enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a team that wins with physical wings, offensive rebounding, turnover creation, and balanced scoring, but the profile also shows very specific pressure points. Their full-season numbers through March 10 show 80.3 points per game, 38.3 rebounds, 16.0 assists, 11.9 turnovers, 8.0 steals, and a +3.5 rebounding margin. They attempt threes at a high rate: 917 of 2,014 field-goal attempts came from three, a 45.5% 3PA/FGA rate, while their offensive rebounding rate is 34.77%, top-60 nationally by RotoWire. Tempo-wise, RotoWire lists Troy at 69.8 possessions per game, and TeamRankings lists them at 74.7 possessions per game in its possession model, so this is not a crawl team; they are most comfortable in a medium-fast game with extra possessions created by the glass and live-ball defense rather than a pure half-court execution grind. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/4/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Style-of-play diagnosis: Troy’s offense is more collective than isolation-heavy in its base structure. The box-score evidence is strong: 527 assists on 905 made field goals means assists on 58.2% of makes, and their 1.3 assist/turnover ratio is solid. Victor Valdes, a 6-7 forward, leads them at 4.6 assists per game, while Cooper Campbell adds 4.2 and Thomas Dowd 2.2, so initiation is spread across multiple bodies instead of one heliocentric guard. Their best offensive games came when the ball moved and they spaced the floor around Dowd’s interior gravity: in the 100-80 win over Texas State on December 31, 2025, Troy shot 61.4% from the field and 62.5% from three, with Cooper Campbell posting 19 points, six assists, and five steals. By contrast, when opponents forced Troy into low-efficiency jump shooting, the offense bogged down badly: against App State on January 31, Troy scored only 44 points, shot 32.7% overall and 14.8% from three; against James Madison on January 29, Troy shot 36.1% and was outrebounded 45-33. The actionable disruption tactic is to shrink driving lanes without overhelping off Cobi Campbell, then finish possessions with one-and-done rebounding. James Madison held Troy to 28 paint points and won the glass by 12; App State held them to four made threes on 27 attempts. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/4/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Press vulnerability: the season-long turnover rate does not scream weakness. RotoWire lists Troy’s offensive turnover rate at 14.58%, and Troy had only 11.9 turnovers per game on the full season. They also posted low-turnover games against quality opposition: six turnovers versus James Madison despite losing, seven versus Akron in a win, seven versus Arkansas State in a win. That means a reckless full-court press is not the primary answer. However, selective pressure after makes can still matter if it is designed to push Troy laterally and consume clock rather than simply hunt steals. In the January 29 loss to James Madison, Troy still only turned it over nine times, but those live-ball miscues were damaging enough to allow 14 Dukes points off turnovers, and JMU repeatedly converted run-outs and paint touches off disrupted actions. The lesson is not “press for volume steals”; it is “use soft containment pressure to keep them out of early offense and force them to initiate at 18 seconds or later.” ([rotowire.com](https://www.rotowire.com/cbasketball/team/troy-1660))

Zone vulnerability: the most direct evidence comes from shot-result games rather than scheme-tag databases. Troy’s offense is vulnerable when a defense can pack the lane, contest above the arc, and make Valdes finish over length instead of as a passer. App State’s January 31 win is the cleanest example of a compact shell causing offensive stagnation: Troy managed only 44 points, 4-of-27 from three, and Thomas Dowd went 1-of-13 overall and 0-of-7 from three. Valdes was held to six points on 2-of-9 shooting. Because Troy relies on Valdes as a frontcourt facilitator and Dowd as a volume rebound-and-finish piece, any zone or matchup-zone that tags Dowd early and stays attached to shooters can expose the lack of elite downhill guard creation. Troy’s best creators are bigger wings/forwards, not a pure paint-touch point guard. Against James Madison, Valdes had 16 points and five assists, but also five turnovers, which is exactly the tradeoff a packed-in, help-heavy coverage wants. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2026/1/31/Troy_vs._App_State__PDF_.pdf))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Troy is at its best when the game gets into the 70s or 80s and their depth/physicality generate accumulation advantages. They won 103-97 in overtime at Kent State, 108-107 in double OT at San Diego State, 106-107 in triple-OT at USC despite losing, 91-65 over Southern Miss, 99-74 over Arkansas State, and 100-80 over Texas State. Those games all fit a possession-rich script. Their worst offensive outputs were 44 against App State, 54 at South Alabama, 59 versus South Alabama, 62 at Texas State, and 63 at LMU. To beat Troy, you need the second script: deny second shots, avoid live-ball turnovers, and make every trip a half-court decision tree. A practical benchmark is to hold them below roughly 70 possessions and under 10 offensive rebounds. If you let them string together transition, free throws, and kick-out threes, they become much harder to manage. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/4/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Size and athleticism by position: PG/lead guard is Cooper Campbell (6-2) or Cobi Campbell (6-2); neither is oversized, so a bigger 6-4 to 6-6 on-ball defender can bother vision and shot release. SG/wing minutes also go to Kameryn Mitchell (6-4) and Austin Cross (6-3), but Troy’s real matchup identity is forward-sized creators: Victor Valdes is 6-7, Kerrington Kiel 6-6, Theo Seng 6-9, Jerrell Bellamy 6-9, and Thomas Dowd 6-8. Dowd averages 14.8 points and 10.1 rebounds; Bellamy shoots 65.1% from the field in a reserve big role; Seng gives them another 12.9 points on 51.7% shooting. That means Troy can overwhelm thin or finesse frontcourts with repeated body blows. The mismatch opportunity against Troy is different: attack their guards with size and force their 6-2 backcourt to switch onto wings, or use a stretch five to drag Dowd/Bellamy away from the rim. App State beat them with perimeter shotmaking from Kasen Jennings, who scored 33 on 11-of-18 shooting and 7-of-11 from three. JMU beat them with frontcourt volume on the glass: Christian Brown had 13 rebounds and Eddie Ricks III had 10, helping produce a 45-33 rebounding edge. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/4/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Isolation vs team offense tendencies: Troy is clearly more team-offense than isolation-offense. The best hard percentage available from public season data is the 58.2% assist rate on made field goals, plus the distribution of playmaking across Valdes (4.6 apg), Cooper Campbell (4.2), and Dowd (2.2). That is not an iso-star profile. Their shooting split also shows why: Valdes, the highest-usage creator, is at 40.1% from the field and 22.3% from three, so their offense is less about clearing a side for efficient one-on-one scoring and more about using Valdes as a connector, Dowd as a screener/rebounder, and Campbell/Campbell as catch-and-shoot or secondary-action guards. In losses to JMU and App State, the assisted ecosystem broke down into harder late-clock attempts: 36.1% shooting against JMU, 32.7% against App State. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2653))

Transition offense and defense: Troy’s 8.0 steals per game and opponent 12.7 turnovers per game show a defense that actively tries to create transition chances, and the play-by-play/box examples confirm it. Against Texas State on December 31, multiple scoring actions were labeled fast break, including Valdes free throws in transition and Dowd/Bellamy rim finishes in early offense. Against App State, despite the loss, Troy still produced 11 fast-break points; against James Madison, both teams scored 11 fast-break points, showing Troy consistently looks to run when given openings. Defensively, the concern is that Troy can be scored on before its size is fully set: App State scored 12 fast-break points and hit 13 threes; JMU got 11 fast-break points and 36 paint points. So the formula is: sprint back after every shot to reduce Troy’s transition offense, then attack their own transition defense before Dowd and Bellamy anchor the paint. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2025/11/4/MBB_2025-26_Season_Stats.pdf))

Coaching adaptability: Scott Cross’s teams do show in-game response capability, but not always enough against the right style. Troy came back from 0-9 down against Akron and took the lead before halftime, then Cooper Campbell scored 19 second-half points in the 79-69 win. The staff also navigated multiple high-variance games successfully, including overtime wins at Kent State and San Diego State and a one-point win at UAB. That suggests solid timeout/halftime adjustment capacity. But the back-to-back home losses to James Madison and App State are the counterexample: when opponents combined physical rebounding with disruptive shot contests, Troy scored 64 and 44 and did not find a late schematic answer. So Cross is adaptable in rhythm games, but the evidence is weaker when the opponent can both win the glass and force jump-shot dependency. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/news/2026/2/10/basketball-m-troy-resumes-conference-play-at-texas-state))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must 1) keep them off the offensive glass by gang-rebounding Dowd, Seng, and Bellamy every possession; 2) prioritize transition floor balance over crashing with extra guards, because Troy’s steals-to-run game is how they reach their preferred tempo; 3) make Valdes a scorer instead of a passer by showing crowded gaps and staying home on Cobi/Cooper Campbell; 4) use size on Troy’s 6-2 guards and involve them in screening actions repeatedly; 5) attack Dowd in space with a stretch big or pick-and-pop five; 6) play disciplined, low-turnover offense, because Troy is good but not unbeatable in the half court if you deny them extra possessions; and 7) if you use pressure, make it tempo pressure, not gambling pressure. The best proof points are the losses: James Madison won 73-64 by rebounding 45-33 and holding Troy to 36.1% shooting; App State won 66-44 by holding Troy to 32.7% overall and 14.8% from three; South Alabama held Troy to 59 and 54 in the two lowest-possession rivalry grinders on Troy’s conference slate. If you make Troy execute in a patient half-court game, you can beat them. If you let them turn the game into a possession battle fueled by steals, second chances, and forward-driven ball movement, they become dangerous. ([troytrojans.com](https://troytrojans.com/documents/download/2026/1/30/Troy_vs._James_Madison__PDF_.pdf))
